takeaways: Navigation that repeats across pages, such as a header, side menu or footer, appears in the same relative order each time, unless the user changes it.
People learn where things are. When the order shifts, they have to find everything again, and some cannot.
“Relative order” means items can be added or removed, as long as the shared items keep their order.
Labeling the same function the same way each time is a different rule, 3.2.4.
failures: Main nav items reordered on different sections
A footer whose links change order from page to page
Search moving before the menu on some pages and after it on others
check: Line up the headers and nav from every template side by side. Do shared items keep their order?
Check the footer and side menus the same way.
Check that any personalised order is something the user chose.

quiz.question: In the account area, a “Billing” link is added to the side nav between existing links. Does this fail 3.2.3?
options: Yes. The nav must be identical on every page
Yes, unless the new link is added at the end
No. The shared links still keep their relative order
quiz.why: The rule is about relative order, not identical menus. Adding a link is fine as long as the links that repeat stay in the same order.

spec: Define the order of every repeated nav block once, in one place.
Show which items may be added on certain sections, and where they go.
Note any user setting that changes the order, so it is the only exception.
review: Is this nav built from the same component as on every other page?
Why is the order different here?
If someone uses this page every day, could they find the menu with their eyes closed?
tradeoff: Each team wants its own section promoted first in the nav. Keep the order fixed and show the current section with a selected state instead.
system: Make headers, nav and footers shared components, so the order is defined once and cannot drift.
pitch: People should not have to relearn our menu on every page. Consistent navigation is faster for everyone.
